summary: The passage classifies post-quantum cryptography (PQC) adoption in digital asset systems along several criteria: where PQC is practical to deploy versus where it will be challenging, and how far cryptographic agility (a platform's capacity to replace algorithms without disrupting operations) helps with migration, compatibility, and swapping weak algorithms. It distinguishes permissionless blockchains, which lack central coordination and need consensus among thousands of nodes, from other systems, and notes immutability as a barrier to rewriting history. It also flags public-key reuse vulnerabilities in Bitcoin and Ethereum. Finally, it differentiates fragmented industry protocols from universally accepted standards, calling for NIST-led common practices in areas such as wallet security, cross-chain bridges, and incident response.

The passage defines "money services business" and "money transmitter" under FinCEN's 2011 rule, and distinguishes the "transmittor" as the sender who initiates a transaction the money transmitter executes. It defines "money transmission services" as accepting value from one person and transmitting it to another by any means. It then clarifies "value that substitutes for currency," which covers value that may not involve currency or funds, and which can be created either for use as a currency substitute or repurposed for that use by an administrator or unincorporated organization. It notes that persons creating such value may fall under other regulatory frameworks, potentially exempting them from MSB status while covering them as a different type of financial institution.

This passage defines "virtual currency" as a medium of exchange that operates like currency but lacks legal tender status, and defines convertible virtual currency (CVC) as a subset that either has equivalent value to currency or substitutes for it. The classification turns on whether an asset functions as value substituting for currency, not on its label, such as "cryptocurrency" or "digital asset." The passage then sets the scope criterion for regulation: transactions in CVC fall under FinCEN rules regardless of whether the token is physical or digital, whether the ledger is centralized or distributed, or what transmission technology is used.

section: Secs. 4-5: Common CVC business models (P2P exchangers, wallets, kiosks, DApps, anonymity-enhanced CVC, trading platforms, ICOs, mining pools)
summary: The passage defines and classifies CVC business models for money transmission purposes, and it sets out how FinCEN's regulations apply to each. It describes P2P exchangers as natural persons trading CVCs, whether regularly or not, and notes the infrequent, non-profit exemption. For wallets, it distinguishes hosted from unhosted wallets and treats the regulatory status of intermediaries by four criteria: who owns the value, where it is stored, whether the owner interacts directly with the payment system, and whether the intermediary has total independent control over the value.

section: Secs. 4-5: Common CVC business models (P2P exchangers, wallets, kiosks, DApps, anonymity-enhanced CVC, trading platforms, ICOs, mining pools)
summary: This FinCEN passage classifies the regulatory treatment of CVC wallet arrangements and kiosks. For hosted wallets, it distinguishes the wallet owner as a user, an agent of the host, or a foreign or domestic financial institution, with each triggering different due diligence duties. It also distinguishes transactions by type and U.S. dollar equivalent, notably "transmittal of funds" subject to the Travel Rule based on the host's position in the chain. Unhosted single-signature wallets are separated from multiple-signature providers, which are money transmitters only if they hold keys in a way that gives them control, combine with hosted services, or record value in their own accounts. CVC kiosks are treated as money transmitters when they accept or dispense currency or CVC.

section: Secs. 4-5: Common CVC business models (P2P exchangers, wallets, kiosks, DApps, anonymity-enhanced CVC, trading platforms, ICOs, mining pools)
summary: This FinCEN passage classifies several CVC business models by whether they qualify as money transmitters under the BSA, using as its main criteria whether an operator accepts and transmits value, whether it is linked to a regulated depository institution, and whether it is integrally tied to the transmission itself. It treats CVC kiosks and DApps that transmit value as money transmitters, regardless of profit motive. For anonymity-enhanced CVC, it distinguishes anonymity-enhanced transactions and privacy coins, and separates providers of anonymizing services (mixers or tumblers, classified as money transmitters) from providers of anonymizing software (not money transmitters). It applies the integral exemption to ask whether a business is distinct from money transmission and whether transmission is necessary for its operation.

section: Secs. 4-5: Common CVC business models (P2P exchangers, wallets, kiosks, DApps, anonymity-enhanced CVC, trading platforms, ICOs, mining pools)
summary: This passage addresses when persons involved with convertible virtual currency fall within the money transmitter definition, using the function and purpose of each activity as the test. It distinguishes suppliers of tools such as communications, hardware, or anonymizing software (exempt as trade) from users who anonymize their own transactions (users, not transmitters) and from those who accept and transmit value for others (transmitters). It classifies anonymity-enhanced CVC providers by payment system type, centralized versus decentralized, and by whether they receive other value or transmit CVC for others. It also covers CVC payment processors and the conditions for the payment processor exemption, including whether the activity facilitates purchases through BSA-regulated clearance systems.

section: Secs. 4-5: Common CVC business models (P2P exchangers, wallets, kiosks, DApps, anonymity-enhanced CVC, trading platforms, ICOs, mining pools)
summary: This passage addresses when CVC payment processors and internet casinos count as money transmitters under the BSA. It sets out the payment processor exemption's conditions, notably whether the processor provides its service under a formal agreement and enters one with the seller who also receives the funds, and whether it operates through a clearing and settlement system admitting only BSA-regulated institutions. It concludes that CVC payment processors generally fall within money transmission, regardless of whether they accept and transmit the same or different types of value. For internet casinos, it covers the definition of a casino by annual gaming revenue and whether conditional bets or payouts constitute money transmission. It ends by introducing exemptions for delivery, communication, and network access services, and for trading platforms.

section: Secs. 4-5: Common CVC business models (P2P exchangers, wallets, kiosks, DApps, anonymity-enhanced CVC, trading platforms, ICOs, mining pools)
summary: This passage distinguishes trading platforms by who takes possession of the convertible virtual currency (CVC) when buyers and sellers are matched. A platform that only posts bids and offers, with or without automatic matching, and leaves settlement to the parties through outside wallets is not a money transmitter; one that buys from sellers and sells to buyers acts as a CVC exchanger and is one. For ICOs, it classifies by business model: a preferential group sale of CVC, where the seller acting as administrator who alone can issue and redeem units is a money transmitter regardless of timing or later migration to decentralized operation; and fundraising through equity or debt tokens to fund projects, whose status depends on whether the actors are MSBs or exempt.

section: Secs. 4-5: Common CVC business models (P2P exchangers, wallets, kiosks, DApps, anonymity-enhanced CVC, trading platforms, ICOs, mining pools)
summary: The passage classifies persons involved in CVC activity by their regulatory status under the Bank Secrecy Act, asking whether each is a money transmitter or MSB. It distinguishes banks, foreign banks, and SEC- or CFTC-registered and functionally regulated persons, whose AML duties flow from other FinCEN rules, from everyone else. For non-excluded persons it asks whether value received in exchange for a new CVC is integral to a sale of goods or services or instead serves as a currency substitute. It separates DApp developers, who are not money transmitters merely by building an application, from users or owners who deploy the DApp for money transmission. Re-sale of tokens creates no BSA duties unless another regime requires broker-dealer or commodity registration. It also addresses CVC creators who pre-mine units and distribute or sell them.

section: Secs. 4-5: Common CVC business models (P2P exchangers, wallets, kiosks, DApps, anonymity-enhanced CVC, trading platforms, ICOs, mining pools)
summary: This passage classifies persons engaged in CVC mining by whether their activity amounts to money transmission under FinCEN rules. Its main criterion is whether a miner uses mined CVC solely to buy goods or services for itself (not an MSB) or uses it to transmit value for others (an MSB). For mining pools and cloud mining, it distinguishes centralized from decentralized pools and treats the leader's or cloud miner's distribution of earned CVC to members or contract purchasers as integral to authentication services, hence not money transmission. The exception is when the leader or cloud miner also hosts wallets for participants, which makes them account-based money transmitters.

section: Part Two: What is a virtual asset? What is a VASP? Scope of the definitions (incl. stablecoins, P2P, DeFi, NFTs)
summary: The passage explains how the FATF defines a virtual asset (VA) and how it relates to other financial assets. A VA is to be read broadly and technology-neutrally, and must be digital, digitally traded or transferred, and usable for payment or investment. Digital records that merely represent ownership of fiat currency or other covered financial assets are excluded, while stablecoins exchangeable at a stable rate may qualify. The key test is whether the asset has inherent value or only records ownership of something else. An asset is not both a VA and a financial asset at once, and jurisdictions choose the designation that best fits their regime, considering commonly accepted usage and the best-fitting regulatory framework.

section: Part Two: What is a virtual asset? What is a VASP? Scope of the definitions (incl. stablecoins, P2P, DeFi, NFTs)
summary: The passage establishes that blockchain-based assets defined as financial assets fall outside this virtual-asset guidance, since the technology is not the deciding factor; every asset for payment or investment must instead be covered as either a VA or another financial asset. For NFTs, it distinguishes unique collectibles (generally not VAs) from NFTs used in practice for payment or investment (which may be VAs) and NFTs representing existing financial assets, applying a case-by-case functional test. Stablecoins are classed as either VAs or financial assets by the same criteria as other digital assets. For VASPs, it lists five activities (fiat exchange, inter-VA exchange, transfer, safekeeping/administration, and issuer-related services) and applies a functional, technology-neutral test that looks to the service actually provided rather than the entity's self-description.

section: Part Two: What is a virtual asset? What is a VASP? Scope of the definitions (incl. stablecoins, P2P, DeFi, NFTs)
summary: The passage defines VASP status by first setting the "as a business" threshold: the actor must act for or on behalf of another natural or legal person, on a commercial basis and with sufficient regularity, so purely internal or infrequent non-commercial transfers fall outside. Having met that test, an entity is a VASP if it performs one of five activities: fiat-to-virtual or virtual-to-fiat exchange, virtual-to-virtual exchange, transfer, safekeeping or administration, and participation in an issuer's offering or sale. The passage classifies these by the actor's role (principal, clearing counterparty, executing facility, or intermediary) and by whether control or ownership of an asset passes to a new party. It also addresses multi-signature arrangements, internal off-chain ledgers, and decentralized applications.

section: Part Two: What is a virtual asset? What is a VASP? Scope of the definitions (incl. stablecoins, P2P, DeFi, NFTs)
summary: This FATF passage addresses when decentralised applications (DApps) and DeFi arrangements fall within the VASP definition. It distinguishes the underlying software, which is not itself a VASP, from the creators, owners or operators who keep control or sufficient influence over the service and provide or actively facilitate VASP services. The criteria include retained control over assets or protocol parameters, an ongoing business relationship with users (even via smart contracts or voting), and whether a party profits from the service. Self-description as "decentralised" is not determinative. Where no controlling person can be identified, the passage suggests monitoring and possible mitigants, such as requiring a regulated VASP's involvement.

section: Part Two: What is a virtual asset? What is a VASP? Scope of the definitions (incl. stablecoins, P2P, DeFi, NFTs)
summary: This passage sets out when entities count as VASPs under the FATF definition, classifying activities by function rather than label. It identifies four categories of exchange and trading services: escrow services where the provider holds custody of funds, brokerage services issuing or trading VAs for users, order-book exchanges (excluding pure matching platforms that perform no listed service), and advanced trading services such as margin or algorithmic trading. It then covers exchange and transfer models, including kiosks. For the custody limb, it asks whether an entity can hold, trade, transfer or spend a VA, or enable control through keys or smart contracts, including multi-signature arrangements. Infrastructure providers, cloud storage firms, and developers or sellers of unhosted wallet software are generally excluded.

section: Part Two: What is a virtual asset? What is a VASP? Scope of the definitions (incl. stablecoins, P2P, DeFi, NFTs)
summary: This passage clarifies when participation in initial coin offerings (ICOs) brings a business within the VASP definition, specifically under limb (v). It distinguishes the act of issuing a virtual asset, which alone is not a covered service, from exchange, transfer, or safekeeping activity carried out on behalf of others, which is. It asks whether a business is affiliated with the issuer and whether it accepts orders, purchases tokens for resale, underwrites, makes markets, or places tokens. It also stresses that substance, not labels, governs categorization, and that the purchaser's intended use (investment or payment) is irrelevant. Creating issuance software alone does not make a developer a VASP. Finally, it notes that the same asset may instead fall under national securities law.

section: Part Two: What is a virtual asset? What is a VASP? Scope of the definitions (incl. stablecoins, P2P, DeFi, NFTs)
summary: The passage clarifies when issuers and other parties fall within the FATF definitions of virtual asset (VA) and VASP. It distinguishes issuers who may be VASPs from those treated as securities issuers, depending on jurisdiction and facts. It separates software developers and platform creators, who are not VASPs merely for building or selling software, from parties who retain control or influence over assets or user relationships, who are. Ancillary providers (hardware wallets, unhosted wallet providers, network infrastructure operators) are excluded unless they facilitate covered activities for others. Closed-loop, non-convertible items and merchant acceptance of VAs are also excluded. The test turns on whether an asset is convertible at market rates and whether a person acts as a business on behalf of others.

section: Part Two: What is a virtual asset? What is a VASP? Scope of the definitions (incl. stablecoins, P2P, DeFi, NFTs)
summary: This passage addresses how the FATF Standards apply to parties in stablecoin arrangements. It distinguishes a central governance body, which is generally covered as a financial institution (FI) or VASP, particularly where it performs other functions, and says such a body should assess ML/TF risks before launch. It notes that some arrangements lack an identifiable VASP or FI, leaving countries to weigh risks and mitigation measures, and that mere software developers are not in scope unless they provide covered financial services. A hypothetical case study (Box 3) then classifies each ecosystem participant (the issuer, Authorised Participants, trading platforms, custodial wallet providers, and reserve-holding FIs) as a VASP or FI or as falling outside the definitions, based on whether its functions involve exchange, transfer, safekeeping, administration, or issuance of the coin.

section: Part Two: What is a virtual asset? What is a VASP? Scope of the definitions (incl. stablecoins, P2P, DeFi, NFTs)
summary: This passage clarifies how the FATF definitions of virtual asset (VA) and VASP apply to a hypothetical stablecoin arrangement and to peer-to-peer (P2P) platforms. It lists parties that generally fall outside VASP status when their functions are limited to validation, cloud hosting, hardware or unhosted-wallet manufacture, merchant sales, or software development without VASP functions, while noting that scrutiny is needed case by case. For P2P platforms, it classifies status by function rather than self-description, distinguishing minimal forum-only services from matching or finding services that may qualify. The criteria it applies include who profits, who sets and changes rules, who controls operations, who launched the service, who keeps the business relationship, and who could shut it down.

section: Annex A: Recommendation 15, Interpretive Note and FATF Definitions; Glossary
summary: The passage defines virtual assets as "property," "proceeds," "funds," or other "corresponding value" for FATF purposes, and sets out who must be regulated as virtual asset service providers (VASPs). It classifies VASPs by their licensing or registration status, distinguishing jurisdictions of incorporation, places of business for natural persons, and offshore service provision. It also exempts entities already licensed as financial institutions with full FATF obligations. Supervision criteria separate competent authorities from self-regulatory bodies, and risk-based supervision powers are specified. Sanctions must be effective, proportionate, and dissuasive, reaching directors and senior management. Preventive measures apply under R.10 (a USD/EUR 1,000 CDD threshold) and R.16 (originator and beneficiary information on virtual asset transfers).

section: Annex A: Recommendation 15, Interpretive Note and FATF Definitions; Glossary
summary: The passage sets out international co-operation duties for virtual assets under Recommendation 15, directing that supervisors of VASPs exchange information with foreign counterparts regardless of their nature, status, or differences in VASP nomenclature. It then defines a virtual asset as a digital representation of value that can be traded or transferred and used for payment or investment, excluding digital representations of fiat currency and securities or other financial assets already covered elsewhere. A virtual asset service provider is defined as a natural or legal person, not covered elsewhere, that as a business conducts one or more of five listed activities for others: exchange between virtual assets and fiat, exchange between virtual assets, transfer, safekeeping or administration, and participation in an issuer's offer or sale. Transfer is defined as a transaction moving a virtual asset from one address or account to another.

section: Section Two: ML/TF/PF Risks (stablecoins, unhosted wallets, offshore VASPs, DeFi)
summary: This passage of the FATF Targeted Update classifies illicit uses of virtual assets by actor and method rather than defining terms. It distinguishes predicate-offence laundering by organised crime, DPRK theft and laundering (including via unregistered VASPs, mixers, bridges and large wallet clusters), cash-for-VA swap networks, fraud and scams (investment "pig butchering", address poisoning, AI-enabled scams), gambling, and terrorist financing. Its criteria are the actor type, the laundering technique, and the reasons for VA use, such as anonymity, speed and fund diversification. The final part examines stablecoins, which are assessed by volume of illicit use, the factors attracting criminals (low volatility, cost and liquidity), and the risk of unhosted-wallet use outside AML/CFT-obliged entities.

section: Section Two: ML/TF/PF Risks (stablecoins, unhosted wallets, offshore VASPs, DeFi)
summary: This passage classifies stablecoin and DeFi risks along several criteria. For stablecoins, it distinguishes issuer models and the programmable features of smart contracts (freezing, blocking, and monitoring of circulation and redemption), and it notes how illicit use is shaped by transfer speed and cost, pairing with mixers, bridges and cross-chain transactions, and dormant or non-trading VASP deposits and withdrawals used for layering. For DeFi, it sorts jurisdictions by whether they require arrangements to be licensed or registered as VASPs, based on whether a creator, owner or operator retains control or sufficient influence. It then tallies whether jurisdictions have registered, sanctioned, identified but not acted against, or found no unregistered DeFi VASPs.

section: Section Two: ML/TF/PF Risks (stablecoins, P2P/unhosted wallets, offshore VASPs, DeFi)
summary: This passage classifies illicit uses of virtual assets by criteria of actor type, typology and convergence. It distinguishes organised crime groups running VA-enabled investment ("pig butchering") fraud from DPRK-affiliated proliferation financing, and identifies the role of each intermediary: a Cambodia-based conglomerate that served both, and Spain's Operation Borrelli, where VAs functioned as both fraud lure and laundering channel. It then sorts cross-cutting risks by shared infrastructure, including stablecoins, offshore intermediaries, OTC brokers, unhosted wallets, bridges, RPC nodes, and Tron-based USDT, and by linked threats: PF, terrorist financing, and sanctions evasion. Its guiding question is whether these typologies stem from weak or uneven FATF implementation, particularly by VASPs in jurisdictions with weak supervision.

section: Section Two: ML/TF/PF Risks (stablecoins, P2P/unhosted wallets, offshore VASPs, DeFi)
summary: The passage defines and classifies several risk categories in the crypto-asset ecosystem and the criteria used to assess them. It identifies AI-enabled virtual asset crime (deepfake recruitment scams, AI-assisted exploit development, open-weight models bypassing commercial safeguards) as a structural amplifier of ML/TF and sanctions-evasion risk. For stablecoins, it distinguishes issuers that retain freeze, block and burn capability from freeze-resistant proprietary designs, judged by whether assets can be frozen under lawful orders. For P2P transactions via unhosted wallets, it assesses visibility, pseudonymity, absence of a reporting obliged entity, and cross-border settlement speed. For offshore VASPs, it defines them by service provision outside their jurisdiction of incorporation or location, and assesses risk by the strength of the home regulatory framework and whether host jurisdictions require licensing or registration.

section: Section Two: ML/TF/PF Risks (stablecoins, P2P/unhosted wallets, offshore VASPs, DeFi)
summary: This passage classifies offshore VASPs (oVASPs) and DeFi arrangements by their risk characteristics and regulatory responses. For oVASPs it distinguishes solicitation tactics, nested access via onshore accounts, and regulatory arbitrage through weak jurisdictions. It asks whether an entity actively serves customers in a jurisdiction, regardless of physical presence, and whether it maintains material local substance such as a compliance officer. For DeFi it asks whether a jurisdiction has identified arrangements meeting the VASP definition, identifying who exercises control or sufficient influence, and whether licensing or registration applies. It also reports survey statistics on DeFi risk assessments, licensing, and enforcement, and cites a targeted report on DeFi regulatory challenges.

This passage sets out how cryptoassets are classified for prudential purposes under the Basel framework. It divides them into Group 1 (those meeting the classification conditions) and Group 2 (those failing them). Group 1 splits into 1a, tokenised traditional assets, and 1b, assets with effective stabilisation mechanisms. Group 2 splits into 2a, assets passing the hedging recognition criteria, and 2b, all others. The key test for Group 1 is whether a tokenised asset carries the same credit and market risk and legal rights as its traditional form, or whether a stablecoin's mechanism is effective at all times in linking its value to reference assets, with redemption rights, monitoring, and verifiable reserves.

This passage sets out the fifth classification condition for stablecoins under the Basel framework and the criteria for two related tests. It requires that a stablecoin pass a redemption risk test and that its issuer be supervised under prudential capital and liquidity rules. The redemption test asks whether reserve assets, net of non-cryptoasset claims, at all times equal or exceed the aggregate peg value, with overcollateralisation where reserves carry extra risk; whether reserves are low-risk, highly liquid assets denominated in peg currencies; and whether governance ensures legally enforceable redemption objectives, operational resilience, public mandates, daily value and weekly composition disclosure, and annual audit. The passage also excludes algorithm-based and cryptoasset-referenced stabilisation mechanisms from condition 1, and sets legal enforceability and five-day redemption for condition 2.

This passage sets out classification conditions for stablecoin-type cryptoassets and the responsibilities for applying them. For stabilisation-mechanism assets, it asks whether arrangements clearly define the redemption rights, redeemer obligations, redemption timeframe, traditional assets exchanged, and how redemption value is set, and whether settlement finality and irrevocability points are documented and publicly disclosed. Condition 3 asks whether the asset's functions and network are designed to manage material risks (credit, market, liquidity, operational, AML/CFT) and whether network elements such as operational structure, access level, node roles, and consensus mechanism are well defined and traceable. Condition 4 asks whether entities executing redemptions, transfers, storage, or settlement are regulated or subject to appropriate risk standards and disclose a governance framework. Finally, it assigns banks ongoing responsibility for classifying exposures into Groups 1a, 1b, 2a, or 2b and documenting and reporting those decisions to supervisors.

This passage addresses the supervisory review of banks' cryptoasset classification decisions, not the classification criteria themselves. It sets out that banks must notify supervisors of classifications with enough lead time for review and possible override, with authorities choosing notification periods based on their resources. It assigns supervisors responsibility for assessing banks' analysis, risk management and classification decisions, permits reliance on other regulators and qualified third-party assessors, and grants supervisors power to override bank classifications consistently, at any time, possibly with a deferred effective date. It also requires routine sharing of supervisory information across jurisdictions to ensure consistent application of the classification conditions.

The passage defines seven terms used in the Basel cryptoasset standard: cryptoassets, digital assets, nodes, operators, stablecoins, redeemers, and validators. It classifies them mainly by their function and structure. Cryptoassets are distinguished as private assets relying primarily on cryptography and distributed ledger technology. Digital assets are separated from digital representations of fiat currency by their payment, investment, or access purposes. Nodes, operators, redeemers, and validators are distinguished by their roles, such as recording data, administering a centralised arrangement, exchanging the asset for traditional value, and committing transaction blocks. Stablecoins are classified by their aim of holding a stable value against a specified asset or basket.

This glossary defines core terms for crypto-asset regulation: blockchain, crypto-asset, and digital asset, along with the actors and activities around them, including issuers, service providers, trading platforms, markets, and the broader ecosystem. It distinguishes stablecoins from global stablecoins by cross-jurisdictional reach and systemic importance, and separates DeFi and DeFi protocols from centralised structures. It classifies wallets by connectivity (hot versus cold) and by control of keys (custodial, held by a provider, versus non-custodial, held by the user). The criteria used throughout are the technology underlying an asset, who issues or provides services, whether a third party controls access to assets, and the asset's stability mechanism and cross-border scale.

section: Annex A: Glossary of Relevant Terms and Definitions
summary: This passage is a glossary defining key crypto-asset terms for the IOSCO report: blockchain, crypto-asset, Crypto-Asset Service Provider (CASP), smart contract, stablecoin, wallet, custodial wallet, and non-custodial wallet. It classifies wallets by two criteria: whether the service provider holds the user's keys (custodial versus non-custodial) and whether the storage is connected to the internet (hot versus cold). It also notes that these definitions are non-legal, scoped to the report, and not intended to enable regulatory arbitrage. The passage also includes Annex B, a feedback statement summarizing 80 consultation responses by stakeholder category, and an excerpt from Recommendation 1 on applying IOSCO standards to crypto-asset activities.

The passage defines key terms of the Convention by classifying data and actors along specific criteria. It distinguishes electronic data, traffic data (defined by origin, destination, route, time, size, duration or service type), content data (everything else relating to the substance of a transfer), and subscriber information (identity, service type and period, and installation location). It defines the ICT system, service provider (by whether it enables communication or stores data for such services), and "property" (including virtual assets). It also covers proceeds of crime, freezing and seizure versus confiscation (temporary versus permanent deprivation), predicate offence, serious crime (a four-year maximum penalty threshold), personal data, regional economic integration organisations, and emergency (significant, imminent risk to life or safety).

The passage defines four terms for the Convention: "computer system," "computer data," "service provider," and "traffic data." It classifies these along functional criteria: whether a device performs automatic processing of data under a program; whether information is represented in a form suitable for computer processing, including programs; whether an entity offers users the ability to communicate by computer system, or stores or processes data for such services; and whether data relates to a communication, is generated by a system in the communication chain, and indicates origin, destination, route, time, date, size, duration, or service type.
